title: Rav Kook's Vision of Peace
hookLine: Rav Kook hoped for a future of gentleness toward animals
carry: the torah's animal laws keep compassion awake
tomorrow: what is the soul reaching for when it longs?
last: RENEW THE OLD, BLESS THE NEW.

lines: A SHOE, OR A CUP AND A POSTCARD?
KINDNESS WIDE ENOUGH FOR EVERY CREATURE.
cards: A spider in the bathtub: some people reach for a shoe, some for a cup and a postcard, to carry it outside. Rav Kook thought about moments like that on a much bigger scale.
His writings on it, gathered by a student under the title A Vision of Vegetarianism and Peace, answer the question with a yes. The hope reaches all the way to the animals.
He pictured a future when human kindness grows wide enough to include every creature.

teach.h: MEAT AFTER THE FLOOD: A CONCESSION.
teach.b: His argument starts in Genesis. In the garden, people are given plants to eat. Only after the flood, in God's words to Noah, is meat allowed.
Rav Kook reads that permission as a concession to a world not yet ready, not the ideal.
And he hears the Torah's smaller laws as practice in gentleness: send the mother bird away before you take her eggs; don't slaughter an animal and its young on the same day.
Jewish law has a name for this concern, tza'ar ba'alei chayim, the suffering of living creatures. These laws keep compassion awake, he teaches, until people are ready for more.
He did not tell his readers to stop eating meat now.

teach.h: A HOPE, NOT A RULE FOR NOW.
teach.b: He spoke of a hope, and of keeping kindness alive on the way there. In his picture, the peace to come takes in the whole of creation, people and animals alike, and nobody is left outside it. Now the week behind it.
A door stripped back to the inner point. An extra soul on Shabbat.
A hidden will, seen looking back.

teach.h: THE TORAH'S ANIMAL LAWS KEEP COMPASSION AWAKE.
teach.b: A rebbe teaching in the dark. God weeping in the inner room. The old renewed, the new made holy.
And a gentleness wide enough for every creature.

how: Jewish law forbids causing animals needless suffering (tza'ar ba'alei chayim); some Jews, drawing on Rav Kook's vision, choose vegetarian meals, while others keep his teaching as a hope for the future and a reason for care in how animals are treated.

o: a rule that every Jew must now eat only plants
a hope that kindness will one day reach every creature
a blessing said over animals before they're fed

games.q: your little brother catches a frog at the creek and wants to keep it in a jar on his desk for good. what would Rav Kook's hope suggest?
o: look at it gently for a while, then let it go home.
keep it; animals are here for people to enjoy.
never touch or look at any wild animal at all.
games.why: Rav Kook hoped kindness would grow wide enough for every creature. the small laws, he taught, keep that compassion awake.

practice: If there's something to eat nearby, hold one bite and smell it before anything else. Then taste it slowly, and think for a moment about where it came from: the field, the hands, the creatures, the water.
Let that one bite be eaten gently, with nothing else going on.

wordCard.voice: Gentleness to all: Rav Kook's hope for a future when human kindness reaches every creature. The last word of the week.

orig.note: Hebrew: the suffering of living creatures; the Jewish principle against causing animals needless pain.

carryVoice: To carry home: the Torah's animal laws keep compassion awake, on the way to a peace wide enough for every creature. That's the week, carried.
